9: My design describes a feature, frequency, distribution or pattern within a defined group or system.
I have stated which group, setting and period my description covers, and what it cannot represent.
I have not invented an intervention simply to make the study seem more scientific.
10: The quantities or categories I describe have clear operational definitions and units where applicable.
I can identify the observational unit and recognise when several records belong to the same unit.
I have not added IV/DV or hypothesis language unless my actual question requires it.
11: I have identified the target population or system and explained whether I observe all of it or a subset.
My measurement procedure produces the variable I claim to describe.
I have considered limits from selection and measurement, alongside any applicable ethics, privacy or safety requirements.
12: Another person could reproduce the descriptive collection procedure.
Each row and column has a defined meaning, and repeated observations remain linked to their source unit.
I have stated how missing observations, data corrections and exclusions will be recorded.
13: I examined missingness and relevant distributions, time patterns or groupings before interpreting the summaries.
The summaries use statistics, counts or proportions appropriate to the variables and observation structure.
14: I have identified the quantity or pattern that answers my descriptive question, including units or denominators where relevant.
The selected summaries or displays suit the variables and preserve relevant grouping or time structure.
Any inference beyond the observed cases is justified by the selection process and applicable assumptions.
15: The Results describe observed values or patterns and make clear who or what was measured.
Every result is traceable to the data or analysis record.
I report differences or changes without treating them as evidence of a causal intervention effect.
16: The Discussion answers the descriptive question directly.
My interpretation reflects the observed cases, measurement conditions and meaningful variation in the data.
I explain how coverage and measurement limitations restrict the conclusions, including any claims beyond the observed units.

9: The key predictor/exposure is measured, not assigned by the researcher.
The design can estimate association/difference/prediction without claiming direct causation.
My question and claim boundary distinguish observed relationships from any proposed causal explanation.
10: The measured predictor and outcome have operational definitions, including their units and observation periods where relevant.
I can identify the observational unit and recognise paired, repeated or clustered records.
I have identified plausible confounders or competing explanations without assuming every associated variable is a confounder.
11: I have explained how cases were selected and how the predictor and outcome were measured.
I have considered who the observed cases represent and how selection could restrict wider inference.
Measurement quality, privacy and any applicable ethics or safety requirements are addressed before data access or collection.
12: The recording plan preserves identifiers needed for paired observations, repeated measures or clustering.
I have documented relevant measurement conditions, plausible sources of bias and any steps intended to reduce them.
The planned analysis matches the observational question and records how missing or excluded data will be handled.
13: I have inspected missingness and relevant distributions and relationships before interpreting the estimates.
The original data are retained, with corrections, recoding and exclusions documented.
I can identify records that share a participant, class, site or other observational unit.
14: I have specified the association, difference or prediction quantity that answers the question, including its scale where relevant.
The method fits the variable types and accounts for pairing, clustering and relevant model assumptions.
I plan to report the main estimate and its uncertainty, rather than relying on a p-value alone.
15: The Results distinguish observed associations or differences from effects attributed to an intervention.
Estimates, uncertainty and any adjustments can be traced to the recorded analysis.
Weak, null and unexpected findings remain visible, together with their estimated magnitude and uncertainty.
16: The answer to my research question reflects the observed relationship or prediction without asserting an untested cause.
I have considered confounding, selection, measurement differences and possible reverse direction where relevant.
Limitations explain how design and sampling restrict causal interpretation and claims beyond the observed cases.

9: I can identify the condition I deliberately assign or manipulate and the units that receive it.
The comparison is clear, including a reference condition or within-unit sequence where appropriate.
I stated the causal claim boundary before seeing results.
10: The assigned factor, measured outcome and timing have clear operational definitions.
I have identified the unit that independently receives treatment and distinguished it from repeated measurements or subsamples.
I can distinguish the comparison condition from the procedures kept consistent across conditions.
11: I have explained how the experimental units were selected and what population or setting they may represent.
Permissions, participant protections and applicable safety precautions are addressed before treatment begins.
The measurement procedure captures the intended outcome and is comparable across conditions where feasible.
12: I count replication at the treatment-assignment level and keep repeated observations linked to their experimental units.
The protocol explains assignment, treatment order, blinding and standardisation where relevant, including protections that are unavailable.
The analysis plan preserves assigned conditions, experimental units and any paired or clustered structure.
13: The original observations retain links between experimental units, assigned conditions and measurement times.
I have examined missing outcomes and relevant distributions within each condition.
Data corrections, exclusions and departures from the planned treatment or procedure are documented.
14: The quantity I want to estimate states the treatment comparison or within-unit contrast, with its scale and units.
The analysis matches the treatment-assignment unit, outcome type and any pairing or repeated structure.
Effect magnitude and uncertainty will be reported.
15: Results identify the units analysed in each condition and trace the treatment contrast to recorded output.
Statistical significance is not treated as effect magnitude.
Missing outcomes, weak or unexpected results and any departures from the protocol remain visible.
16: My interpretation distinguishes the observed treatment contrast from proposed mechanisms that were not directly measured.
I have considered how assignment, adherence, contamination or attrition could affect the interpretation, where relevant.
Claims about other units, populations or settings reflect the conditions actually tested and the study's limitations.

9: I have identified the intervention or change and explained when and how it occurred.
The design provides a meaningful comparison, such as an untreated group or a pre-intervention trend.
I have considered whether other changes could explain the findings.
10: The intervention or exposure, outcome and units of observation have clear definitions and measurement periods.
I have considered baseline differences, time trends and other influences on the comparison.
The reference group or period is justified without assuming nonrandom groups are equivalent.
11: I have explained how people, sites or records were selected and measured.
I have considered baseline differences, timing and changes in the observed population.
Relevant permissions, privacy protections and safety requirements have been addressed.
12: The protocol documents intervention timing, implementation and the units or periods observed.
I have identified what supports the comparison and how competing explanations will be examined.
Missing-data rules, exclusions and departures from the procedure are included in the plan.
13: I have inspected missing observations, relevant baseline patterns and changes around the intervention.
The original records remain available, with corrections and implementation differences documented.
I can trace groups, sites or periods and recognise repeated or clustered records.
14: The analysis estimates the intended comparison without treating adjustment as randomisation.
The analysis checks assumptions relevant to this design, including time trends, clustering or time dependence where applicable.
The estimated contrast and its uncertainty will be reported with a suitably qualified interpretation.
15: The Results identify the units, groups or periods contributing to the estimates.
The Results do not claim randomisation that did not occur.
Weak or contradictory findings are reported.
16: I have considered whether selection, concurrent events or other changes could account for the findings.
Causal wording is calibrated to the actual quasi-experimental design.
Limitations explain how the comparison, measurement and coverage restrict the conclusions.

9: The design matches a question about meaning, experience, process, explanation, or context.
I stated what kind of qualitative evidence will answer the question.
My claims remain grounded in the studied setting and evidence, within boundaries suited to this approach.
10: I have described the phenomenon and relevant domains in terms that fit the question.
I distinguish the participant or case from the excerpt, observation or other evidence record.
I have stated what will count as relevant evidence.
11: I have explained which cases to include, why they fit the question and how access will be arranged.
The planned conversations, observations or documents can provide evidence relevant to the question.
I have considered participant protections and how my relationship to the setting could shape the evidence.
12: The procedure explains how evidence is collected, organised and linked to its source.
My approach to interpretation is explained, with room to document changes as understanding develops.
I have planned for missing or withdrawn material, confidentiality and documented exclusions.
13: The original qualitative corpus is preserved.
Transcription, annotation, corrections and analytic changes remain traceable without altering the original record.
The corpus summary describes what was collected and helps me examine variation before settling on findings.
14: I have explained how the chosen approach develops findings through coding, close reading or another justified process.
I have described how interpretations and analytic decisions will be examined, using quality checks suited to the method.
I am not adding a p-value or effect-size requirement that the qualitative question does not need.
15: Each central finding is supported by relevant excerpts, observations, documents or other evidence.
My interpretive reasoning is visible while participants' words and actions remain accurately represented.
Different accounts, tensions and boundary cases are considered where relevant.
16: The Discussion answers the qualitative question in context.
I have considered how the setting and my research decisions may have shaped the interpretation.
I explain where findings may be informative and what the available evidence leaves uncertain.

9: The review design matches a question answered from existing research.
I have identified whether the review maps, critically examines or synthesises evidence, and what its scope allows.
The claim boundary reflects how sources were found, selected and interpreted.
10: I have defined the concepts and contexts of interest and distinguished reports from the studies or other sources they describe.
I use terms suited to the review question without imposing experimental variables or participant recruitment.
The eligibility criteria can be applied to the types of sources I intend to include.
11: The search and selection approach is explained in enough detail for the stated review type.
I have planned how information will be extracted or recorded and whether critical appraisal suits this review.
I can explain which literature the search may miss and how that limits claims about the field.
12: The procedure documents searching, selection, extraction and synthesis, with deduplication where needed.
The evidence matrix identifies what each row represents and links multiple reports of the same study where relevant.
I have explained how unclear or unreported information, exclusions and changes in decisions will be recorded.
13: Original search and source records are retained so that selection and extraction decisions remain traceable.
The evidence summary distinguishes records, reports and studies when their counts differ.
Corrections to extraction or selection decisions are documented without obscuring the earlier record.
14: The synthesis method explains how evidence will be compared or brought together to answer the review question.
I have examined differences in methods, populations and evidence quality to the extent appropriate for this review.
Any statistical synthesis is justified by the question and data; a narrative or scoping review need not produce a pooled estimate.
15: The Results identify the scope of included evidence and describe what the synthesis found.
Interpretations and patterns can be traced to their supporting studies or other included sources.
I do not treat diverse findings as one numerical effect unless a defensible analysis supports it.
16: The discussion answers the review question using what the included evidence can support.
I explain how search coverage and limitations of the included evidence affect interpretation.
Any claim that research is absent or insufficient remains bounded by the search and selection process.

9: The question requires quantitative synthesis of existing comparable effects.
I stated the scope of studies/effects and claim boundary.
I understand that meta-analysis still depends on study quality and comparability.
10: Treatment/exposure, outcome/effect metric, eligibility concepts, and independent effect unit are defined.
Multiple effects from the same sample will not automatically be treated as independent.
The effect definition matches the review question.
11: Search, screening, extraction, and appraisal procedures are planned.
Coverage/generalization limits of the included literature are explicit.
Effect-size information can be obtained or converted consistently.
12: Effect extraction/conversion and dependence rules are prespecified.
One effect-size row and all variance/SE/study-ID fields are defined.
Missing-statistic and duplicate-sample decisions are documented.
13: Extracted effects and study characteristics are checked before pooling.
Corrections and conversions are traceable to source reports.
14: The pooled estimand/effect metric and model are defined.
Heterogeneity, dependence, sensitivity, and moderator decisions are justified.
Pooled magnitude and uncertainty are central; p-values are secondary.
15: Results report pooled estimate, uncertainty, study count/effect count, and heterogeneity where appropriate.
Forest/other outputs are traceable to extracted effects.
Sensitivity or conflicting evidence is reported transparently.
16: Interpretation accounts for heterogeneity, bias, study quality, and dependence.
The pooled estimate is not generalized beyond represented populations/outcomes/designs.
Limitations distinguish meta-analytic model limits from primary-study limits.

9: I can explain why one evidence type alone is insufficient.
The quantitative and qualitative strands each answer a defined part of the question.
I stated how the strands will relate or integrate.
10: Quantitative variables and qualitative phenomena/domains use appropriate terminology for their own strand.
The unit(s) represented in each strand are clear.
I have not forced the qualitative strand into IV/DV language.
11: Sampling, collection quality, ethics, and generalization/transferability are considered for both strands.
The two strands have compatible case linkage where integration requires it.
Each measure/procedure supports its intended interpretation.
12: Both strand procedures and data structures are documented.
The integration point is stated before final interpretation.
Missing/exclusion/coding rules are explicit for each evidence type.
13: Quantitative data and qualitative corpus are each quality-checked before integration.
IDs/linkage are preserved when the same cases contribute both strands.
Early summaries do not collapse one evidence type into the other.
14: Each strand uses an analysis appropriate to its evidence type.
The integration method explains how results will be connected, compared, or merged.
Quantitative significance is not used to override contradictory qualitative evidence automatically.
15: Results distinguish quantitative, qualitative, and integrated findings.
Each finding is traceable to its evidence source.
Convergence and divergence between strands are reported.
16: The Discussion explains what the strands jointly add.
Contradictions between strands are analyzed rather than hidden.
Limitations address both strand-specific and integration-specific weaknesses.
